column2: Read README.txt, then read every regional sales file it lists in a single step, issuing all of those reads together rather than one after another. If a read fails, say which file it was and carry on with the others. For each region you could read, compute the total units and the total revenue (units times unit_price, summed over its rows), then the same two totals over all of those regions, and name the region with the highest revenue per unit sold. Do the arithmetic yourself from the file contents, without writing or running a script, and do not create or change any files. Answer with a small table followed by that region's name.

This workspace has a settings loader, loader.py, and layered settings files under settings/. Read loader.py to learn which layers it applies, in what order, and how each kind of line changes the result. Then read the layer files, all of them in one step where your tools allow it; the loader skips a layer whose file does not exist, so if a read fails, note it and go on. Work out the effective settings of the [server] and [cache] sections once every layer has been applied, without running any code, and answer with one line per key in the form section.key = value. If your harness can start sub-agents, you may hand the reading of the layer files to one; otherwise do everything yourself. Do not modify any files.

Run the test suite with `python3 -m unittest -v` from the workspace root; some of the tests fail. The tests are correct, so find the cause in wordstats.py, fix it with the smallest change that makes sense, and run the suite again until every test passes. Then report which tests failed at first, what the bug was, and how many tests pass at the end.

The three modules in reports/ (daily.py, weekly.py and monthly.py) each carry their own copy of the same rounding helper, _round_half_up. Move it into a new module, reports/util.py, as a public function named round_half_up; make the three modules import it from there and delete their copies; and add a one-line entry about the change to the unreleased section of CHANGES.txt. Run `python3 -m unittest -v` before you start (one test module fails because reports/util.py does not exist yet) and again when you are done, when every test must pass. Finish by listing the files you changed or created and the number of tests that ran.

Run `python3 make_data.py` first; it writes station.log, a service log of 3,000 lines. Then read station.log from the first line to the last, 200 lines per read, with your file-reading tool (or `sed -n` if you only have a shell). Do not grep, count, sort or parse it with a script or a one-liner: the point of this task is to read it. Keep your notes in findings.md: after each part, and before you read the next one, append every WARN and ERROR line of that part (time, node, level and message) and update the file's first line to say how many lines you have read so far. If your context gets compacted, carry on from findings.md rather than from memory. When you have read the last line, answer from findings.md: how many WARN lines and how many ERROR lines the log has, which node logged the most of them, and the sum of the dropped= values over all ERROR lines.

Run `python3 make_data.py` to create orders.csv (2,500 orders), then run `python3 report.py orders.csv`; it crashes on some of the rows. Look at the rows it fails on. Then change report.py so that load_orders skips every row it cannot parse and returns the parsed orders together with the number of rows it skipped, and so that the report ends with a line `skipped rows: N`, as tests/test_report.py expects. Run `python3 -m unittest -v` until every test passes, run the report on orders.csv again, and answer with the revenue per category, the grand total and the number of skipped rows it printed.

Add a `--precision` option to the length converter in this workspace: a non-negative integer number of decimal places for the printed result, 2 by default, with a negative value rejected as a usage error. Parse it in convert/cli.py, apply it in format_result in convert/units.py, document it in USAGE.txt, and add tests for it to tests/test_cli.py, one of them for a negative value. Keep the existing tests passing and run the whole suite with `python3 -m unittest -v`. Finish by showing the output of `python3 -m convert 10 km mi --precision 4`.

rotate.sh is meant to keep the newest KEEP snapshot files in a directory, newest by the date in their names, and to delete the older ones, but its tests fail. Run `bash test_rotate.sh` to see which checks fail, fix rotate.sh (the test script is correct, so leave it alone), and run the tests again until every check passes. Then explain in two or three sentences what was wrong.
